note: Shows basic subject structure. "Apfel" is masculine (der), so the indefinite article in nominative is "ein".
"Der" confirms masculine gender. Adjectives sitting after "ist" (predicate adjectives) take no inflectional endings.
Proper nouns in German take an -s suffix for possession without an apostrophe (Johns).

en: I must give it to him.
note: The modal verb "muss" takes position 2, kicking the main infinitive "geben" to the end. Masculine accusative pronoun "ihn" ("it") vs dative "ihm" ("him").
Because "apple" is the direct object (accusative masculine), "sein" gains an -en ending to become "seinen".
The strong verb "geben" undergoes a stem vowel change in 3rd person singular: e → i (er gibt).
"Uns" serves as the dative "to us". Direct object pronoun (ihn) precedes indirect object pronoun/noun.
"Ihr" is feminine dative ("to her"); "den Apfel" is masculine accusative direct object.
When negating a specific direct object action, "nicht" moves toward the end of the clause.

en: They want to give it to me.
note: When both objects are pronouns, Accusative (ihn) comes before Dative (mir).

en: But I do not want the apple either.
de: Aber ich will den Apfel auch nicht.
note: "Aber" is a position-zero conjunction; it does not alter standard Verb-Second (V2) word order. "Auch nicht" means "neither/not either".

de: Ich kann den Apfel nicht essen.
note: The conjugated modal "kann" sits at position 2, while "nicht" precedes the sentence-final infinitive "essen".
Translates "it" as "er" (masculine) because it refers to "der Apfel". Independent possessive pronoun takes masculine ending -er.
Many masculine nouns add an umlaut in the plural: Apfel → Äpfel. The possessive adds -e for plural (meine).

en: I will not take the red apple.
de: Ich werde den roten Apfel nicht nehmen.
note: Future tense formed with auxiliary "werden" + final infinitive. "Roten" receives -en ending due to weak masculine accusative declension.
Questions swap verb and subject, placing the conjugated verb (möchtest) in position 1.
"Welcher" declines like a definite article. Since it replaces a masculine accusative noun, it becomes "welchen".

en: I will give you the red apple.
de: Ich werde dir den roten Apfel geben.
note: "Werde" (position 2) controls the sentence, sending "geben" to the very end. Dative object "dir" precedes accusative object "den roten Apfel".
"War" is the simple past 3rd-person singular of "sein" (to be).

en: But he said he doesn't want it anymore.
de: Aber er hat gesagt, dass er ihn nicht mehr will.
note: Subordinating conjunction "dass" forces the conjugated verb "will" to the absolute end of the clause.
Adverb "jetzt" occupies position 1, forcing verb "gehört" to position 2 before subject "er". "Gehören" requires a dative object (dir).
"Solltest" uses Konjunktiv II to render advice ("should") rather than absolute command.
Standard spoken past uses auxiliary "haben" in position 1 and past participle "gegessen" at the end.

de: Warum hast du ihn nicht gegessen?
note: Question word "warum" in position 1, auxiliary "hast" in position 2, participle "gegessen" at the end.

en: If you ate it, you would be happy.
de: Wenn du ihn essen würdest, wärst du glücklich.
note: "Wenn" clause puts "würdest" at the end. The whole wenn-clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts immediately with the verb "wärst".

en: Now someone else will eat the apple.
de: Jetzt wird jemand anderes den Apfel essen.
note: Time adverb "jetzt" triggers inversion: jetzt (1) + wird (2) + subject (3).

en: They will eat all of the apples.
note: "Alle" precedes uninflected plural noun "Äpfel" directly without needing "of".

en: And there are a lot of apples to eat.
de: Und es gibt viele Äpfel zu essen.
note: "There are" is rendered as "es gibt" (+ Accusative). Purpose structure uses "zu" + infinitive.

de: Die meisten von ihnen sind rot.
note: "Die meisten" acts as a substantive superlative. Preposition "von" demands dative pronoun "ihnen".

en: But some of them are green.
de: Aber einige von ihnen sind grün.
note: "Einige" functions as "some/several" for countable plural items.

en: And none of the apples are blue.
de: Und keiner der Äpfel ist blau.
note: "Der Äpfel" is genitive plural ("of the apples"). Negative pronoun "keiner" is singular, taking singular verb "ist".

en: A few of them are big.
de: Ein paar von ihnen sind groß.
note: Lowercase "ein paar" means "a few/some" (as opposed to capitalized "ein Paar" meaning a literal pair/two).

en: And one of the apples is very small.
de: Und einer der Äpfel ist sehr klein.
note: "Einer" takes masculine ending -er to stand in for "ein Apfel". Combined with genitive plural "der Äpfel".

en: But all of the apples are beautiful.
note: Demonstrates direct modification where "alle" directly precedes the subject without prepositions.

en: These are beautiful, big, red apples.
de: Das sind schöne, große, rote Äpfel.
note: When no determiner precedes a plural noun in nominative, every adjective receives the strong plural -e ending.

en: You can have as many as you want.
de: Du kannst so viele haben, wie du willst.
note: Equative comparative "so [viele] … wie …" ("as many as"). Secondary clause sends "willst" to the end.

en: Because I have enough for everyone.
de: Weil ich genug für alle habe.
note: Subordinating conjunction "weil" sends conjugated verb "habe" to the absolute end. Preposition "für" demands accusative "alle".
"Jeder" ("everyone/each person") is grammatically singular, taking singular verb "mag" (from mögen).

en: The biggest ones are the best.
note: Superlative adjectives (groß → größt) drop their noun and act as primary subjects taking plural weak -en endings.
Plural noun without article requires strong adjective ending -e (kleine).

en: But the big apples are better.
de: Aber die großen Äpfel sind besser.
note: Comparative form of "gut" is irregular (besser). Attributive adjective after "die" takes weak plural -en ending (großen).
